name: False Memory
description: People can remember events or details that never happened, or remember them in materially distorted form. False memories can arise from suggestion, associative lure, imagination, or source confusion rather than deliberate lying.
design_relevance_note: Relevant mainly as a research and evidence-quality caution: retrospective interviews, support reports, incident narratives, and post-hoc explanations of product behavior can contain confident but incorrect remembered details. This is not a general-purpose interface-design law.
prevalence_note: Much more publicly recognizable than most Tier C memory terms and relevant to research, trust, and legal discussions, but still not part of the core named digital-product design canon.

findings.description: Reviewing the false-memory literature, Roediger and McDermott argue that normal associative memory processes can produce confident recollection of items or events that were never actually experienced, rather than false memory requiring deception or pathology.

The same review concludes that people can come to believe falsely that they experienced rich, complex events that never in fact occurred, showing that false memory can extend beyond minor detail distortion to invented episodes under some conditions.
findings.source_title: Planting misinformation in the human mind: a 30-year investigation of the malleability of memory.

applications.title: The False Memory Syndrome Foundation: a scientific concept mobilized into a legal-defense strategy
applications.description: New York Magazine's investigative feature documents how, after psychology professor Jennifer Freyd privately accused her father Peter Freyd of childhood sexual abuse in 1990, her parents Pam and Peter Freyd responded by founding the False Memory Syndrome Foundation (FMSF) in 1992. The foundation popularized the term 'false memory' as an organized framework for casting doubt on sexual-abuse allegations broadly, not only in the Freyds' own case. Per the article's reporting, the foundation operated from 1992 until it abruptly shuttered in December 2019, and the false-memory framework it promoted went on to be invoked in defense strategies in several high-profile sexual-abuse cases, including those of Michael Jackson, Bill Cosby, and Harvey Weinstein.
applications.industry_context: legal defense strategy in sexual-abuse litigation; nonprofit advocacy
applications.ethical_note: A real scientific finding (memory can be distorted or fabricated under certain conditions) was organized into an advocacy framework that the source documents as being used, at scale, to cast systematic doubt on sexual-abuse survivors' testimony -- a serious, well-documented instance of a genuine cognitive-science concept being deployed in a way that caused real harm to real people, not a hypothetical ethics-course example.
